a: the outer gate of the sanctuary
p: The guide brings Ezekiel back to the gate by which the glory came in (43:1-5).
b: The gate that faces east is the one the glory of the LORD entered in 43:1-5, coming back the way it left (10:18-19; 11:22-23). Ezekiel is now standing in the outer court, looking at it from inside. Chapter 44 starts from what the glory's entry did to the gate. The next verses say what that means for the gate, for who may stand near the glory, and for the people who serve there.

p: Jewish, Christian and critical readers explain the shut gate in different ways.
b: Rashi, following the Mishnah, says the verse means the little south door of the Temple's great gate, which no one ever used (Rashi cites the tractate Middot). Radak gives the plain reading and the rabbis' reading and adds that the entry meant is the glory's. Ambrose and later Catholic and Orthodox writers read the gate as Mary, shut before and after the birth of Christ (see the card below). Many modern commentators, such as Zimmerli and Block, take it as a sign that the LORD's return is final and the way he came is now holy ground.

t: Nasi: the leader, not the prince
p: Ezekiel's word for the future ruler is nasi, and he almost never says king.
b: Nasi comes from nasa', 'lift up', so a 'lifted' or chosen head. The KJV and many versions say 'prince'; this Plain says 'the leader', as at 12:10 and 34:24. Ezekiel uses 'king' of the coming ruler only in 37:22 and 37:24, and in 34:24 and 37:25 David is the nasi. In chapters 44-48 the leader has a seat, land and duties but no priestly rights: he may not offer the sacrifices himself (46:2) and he keeps off the altar. How this ruler relates to 'David my servant' of 34:23-24 is debated.

p: 'Eat bread' is a meal; the verse does not say what food.
b: 'Eat bread' is Hebrew for 'share a meal'. The verse does not say what the leader eats. Many commentators think it is his share of a peace offering, eaten in the gateway chamber (compare Exodus 24:11 and Leviticus 7:15-21), which fits his duty to supply offerings (45:17). The Hebrew text has an unusual form of the verb 'to eat' that the written text and its marginal reading spell differently. The sense is not affected.

a: The glory of the LORD had filled the house of the LORD
t: The glory fills the house again
p: The same scene as the opening of the Tabernacle and Solomon's Temple.
b: The glory 'filled' the Tabernacle when Moses finished it (Exodus 40:34-35) and Solomon's Temple when the priests came out (1 Kings 8:10-11). Ezekiel last saw it leave in 11:23, and it came back in 43:1-5. Here he sees it a second time from the north gate, and falls on his face as he did at 1:28 and 3:23. The 'glory of the LORD' (kavod YHWH) is the book's way of saying that the LORD himself is present, not an object. The root of the word means 'heavy'.

p: A Hebrew idiom for giving full attention, not a command about feelings.
b: The Hebrew says 'set your heart', then 'see with your eyes' and 'hear with your ears'. In Hebrew the heart is the place of thinking and choosing, so this is a call to concentrate. The same three-part call opens the Temple tour in 40:4 and 43:10-11. What follows is a list of rules that Ezekiel is to learn and pass on. The word for 'rules' here is chuqqot and for 'laws' torot, the plural of torah in its sense of 'instruction'.

p: Ezekiel's usual phrase is 'rebellious house'; here the Hebrew has a different form.
b: Elsewhere this Plain says 'rebellious house' every time (beit meri: 2:5-8; 3:9, 26-27; 12:2-3, 9, 25; 17:12; 24:3). Here the Hebrew has el-meri, 'to the rebellious one', and the Plain keeps that wording instead of changing it to the usual phrase. Swete's Greek has the usual 'rebellious house'; see the variant.

a: people uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh
p: Uncircumcised outsiders working inside the Temple: scholars disagree who they were.
b: The charge is that uncircumcised foreigners were brought into the sanctuary to share its work. No other book names this practice, so its details are debated. One view takes them as foreign slaves or guards who did menial work, like the Gibeonites who became wood-cutters and water-carriers for the altar (Joshua 9:23, 27) or the temple servants listed in Ezra 2:43-54. Another sees palace guards of foreign origin (compare 2 Kings 11:4). Another takes the charge as figurative for Israelites who were 'uncircumcised in heart' (Jeremiah 9:26). Block and Levenson discuss these options.

t: The altar as the LORD's table
p: Sacrifices are called the LORD's 'food', and the altar his 'table' (44:16).
b: Leviticus calls the offerings 'the food of God' (Leviticus 21:6; 3:11), and 44:16 speaks of 'my table'. Israel's prophets knew this language could be misunderstood as if the LORD needed to eat (Psalm 50:12-13). It is best taken as the language of hosting: the sacrifice is the LORD's meal, served in his house, and priests and offerers share it.

a: keep your charge over my holy things
p: Guard duty over the holy things, which the priests had handed on to others.
b: Mishmeret means a duty of guarding or watching. In the law the Levites 'guard' the Tabernacle so that no outsider comes near and wrath falls on Israel (Numbers 1:53; 3:7-8; 18:3-5). The charge here is that the priests did not do this themselves, but 'appointed others, for yourselves', to do it. Swete's Greek reads more simply that they 'ordered guard duties' in the holy places. This Plain uses 'charge' every time (44:14, 15, 16; 48:11).

p: A mocking name for idols, used about 39 times in Ezekiel.
b: Gillulim is Ezekiel's favorite word for idols (6:4-6; 8:10; 14:3-7; 20:7 and on). It sounds like gelel, 'dung pellets', and probably means 'dung-things', a mocking name that Swete's Greek does not carry over (eidola). The Plain uses 'filthy idols' every time. Ezekiel also uses shiqqutsim, 'detestable things', and to'evot, 'abhorrent things', and those are three different words that this Plain keeps apart. Here 'filthy idols' tells us what the Levites served: the shrines away from Jerusalem, as the next verse says.

a: the Levites who moved far from me
t: The Levites demoted: history or ideal?
p: Wellhausen read this as the origin of the priest and Levite divide; later scholars dispute it.
b: In the law all the tribe of Levi serves, but only Aaron's family are priests (Numbers 16-18). In Deuteronomy any Levite may be a priest (Deuteronomy 18:6-8). Wellhausen argued that Ezekiel here invents the lower class of Levites by demoting the country priests of the high places after Josiah's reform, which closed those shrines (2 Kings 23:8-9). Haran and Milgrom, who date the priestly laws before Ezekiel, argue instead that the duties of priests and Levites were already distinct, so that Ezekiel works from them. Block and Levenson give other versions. The text itself says only that these Levites served idolatrous shrines.

a: raised my hand in an oath
p: The gesture of an oath, as at 20:5 and Exodus 6:8.
b: Literally 'I lifted up my hand against them'. Lifting the hand is the gesture of an oath (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40), and in Ezekiel the LORD swears with it both for good, as in 20:5-6, and for ill, as here and in 20:23. Swete's Greek has a similar phrase. Behind the oath is the sentence: they 'will bear their guilt', the same phrase Leviticus uses for a penalty that falls on the person.

p: Priests of Zadok's line, promoted here; the name lives on in the Qumran sect and the Sadducees.
b: Zadok served David and anointed Solomon, who made him the priest in place of Abiathar (2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Kings 1:39; 2:35). Ezekiel names his sons as the only priests who may come near the altar (40:46; 43:19; 48:11). The Qumran community's Damascus Document quotes this verse and reads the 'sons of Zadok' as the elect of the last days. The name of the Sadducees is usually derived from Zadok too (a derivation that is debated). The Chronicler's genealogies place Zadok in Aaron's line through Eleazar (1 Chronicles 6:50-53).

p: Linen is the priestly cloth in Exodus and Leviticus; wool is kept out.
b: The high priest wore linen when he entered the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:4), and all priests wore linen undershorts (Exodus 28:42). Ezekiel makes linen the rule for every priest in the inner court and bans wool (compare Leviticus 19:19 on mixed cloth). Exodus 28 has blue, purple and scarlet yarn (usually taken to be wool) woven into the high priest's garments, so Ezekiel's rule is stricter and simpler. The next verse says why: nothing that makes them sweat.

p: The text gives no reason for the ban; sweat is the only trace of a reason.
b: The Hebrew is 'they will not gird themselves with sweat'. The text does not say why. Suggestions include that sweat means effort and toil, which does not suit service in the LORD's presence; that sweat is a body fluid that carries impurity; and that tight belts of wool make a person sweat. Swete's Greek has a different word here (it can mean 'by force').

p: In the priestly system, holy things can pass holiness to what touches them.
b: In the priestly laws holiness could be passed on by touch: whatever touched a sin offering's flesh became holy (Leviticus 6:27) and the clothes needed washing. Ezekiel 42:14 already tells the priests to leave their clothes in the holy rooms. Here the aim is that ordinary people not be burdened with holiness they have no preparation to handle (Haggai 2:11-12 asks the priests a related question). The Hebrew text has the phrase 'to the outer court' twice in this verse; Swete's Greek has it once, and so does the Plain.

a: They must keep the hair of their heads trimmed
p: Neither shaved (as in mourning) nor wild (as for a Nazirite).
b: Leviticus bars priests from shaving their heads in mourning (Leviticus 21:5) and tells Aaron's sons not to let their hair go loose when his sons died (Leviticus 10:6). A Nazirite let the hair grow long as a sign of his vow (Numbers 6:5). Ezekiel steers a middle course. The verb 'trim' (kasam) occurs only here and its meaning is uncertain; Swete's Greek has 'cover their heads'.

p: The same ban as Leviticus 10:9, set in the inner court.
b: After Nadab and Abihu died, the LORD told Aaron that he and his sons must not drink wine or beer when they went into the tent of meeting (Leviticus 10:9), so that they could tell the holy from the common. Ezekiel puts the same rule in the inner court and gives it in a list with the teaching duty of 44:23, which is the reason Leviticus gives too.

a: or else the widow of another priest
p: Ezekiel is stricter than Leviticus for ordinary priests, and looser than for the high priest.
b: Leviticus bars an ordinary priest from marrying a woman who has been made common or a divorced woman, and the high priest from marrying a widow as well (Leviticus 21:7, 13-14). Ezekiel bars every priest from marrying a widow or a divorced woman but lets him marry the widow of a priest.

p: The priests are the court for disputes inside the Temple and the people.
b: Deuteronomy sends hard cases to 'the Levite priests' and a judge at the chosen place (Deuteronomy 17:8-9; 19:17), and Jehoshaphat set up priests as judges in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 19:8-10). Ezekiel makes it a duty of the Zadokites. Swete's Greek reads 'a case of bloodshed'. The priests' part in judging fits the limited powers given to the leader in 45:8-9.

a: a sister who has never had a husband
p: Leviticus lists the same close relatives; Ezekiel adds a seven-day wait and an offering.
b: Leviticus lets a priest touch the dead only for close relatives: mother, father, son, daughter, brother and an unmarried sister (Leviticus 21:1-3). That list does not name a wife. Ezekiel's list is the same, and he too leaves out a wife, whose death he himself faced in 24:15-18, where he was told not to mourn. Verses 26-27 add a seven-day wait and a sin offering after contact with the dead, which Leviticus 21 does not mention; Numbers 6:9-12 and 19:11-19 have similar rules.

t: The LORD as the priests' share
p: The Levites' and priests' answer to having no land (Numbers 18:20).
b: The tribe of Levi received no land of its own; the LORD told Aaron, 'I am your portion and your inheritance' (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 18:1-2; Joshua 13:33). Ezekiel repeats this and then, in 45:1-5 and 48:10-12, gives the priests and Levites a holy district. The district is not a tribal inheritance but a holy place for the sanctuary and the priests' houses (45:4).

p: Not 'under the ban' here: a thing given outright to the LORD.
b: Cherem usually means 'under the ban', set apart for destruction (Joshua 6:17-18). In priestly law it also covers a thing 'devoted' to the LORD that can never be bought back, and such things belong to the priests (Leviticus 27:21, 28; Numbers 18:14). That is the sense here.

p: The Torah forbids this food to everyone; why does Ezekiel address priests only?
b: Leviticus forbids priests to eat an animal that died on its own or was torn (Leviticus 22:8), and the law elsewhere lets a resident foreigner eat it but sets a purity penalty for an Israelite (Leviticus 17:15; Deuteronomy 14:21). Menachot 45a takes up this verse when it asks whether only priests are forbidden a carcass or a torn animal, since the Torah bans it for all; Rabbi Yochanan calls the passage difficult and says Elijah will explain it in the future. One common answer is that priests are held to a stricter standard. Compare Ezekiel 4:14, where Ezekiel said he had never eaten such meat.

p: A hard-to-translate word for a portion lifted out for the LORD; the Plain says 'contribution'.
b: Terumah comes from rum, 'raise', and is a portion lifted off a larger whole and given to the LORD (Leviticus 7:14; Numbers 18:8-19). Here it is a district of land. The Plain says 'contribution' (as in Leviticus 7:14) and, for the land, 'holy contribution'. The same word names the gifts of grain and oil in 45:13-16.

a: divide the land as an inheritance
p: The verb is 'make fall': casting lots, as in Numbers 26:55.
b: The Hebrew verb here and in 47:14, 22 is 'make fall', the language of the lot (Numbers 26:55-56; Joshua 18:6, 8). The land was to be divided by lot, and yet Ezekiel fixes the order of the tribes in advance (48:1-7, 23-27), so 'lot' may be only a figure of speech for dividing. The 'equal' strips of 47:14 also depart from Numbers, where larger tribes got larger shares (Numbers 26:54).

t: How big is a cubit here?
p: The measures are in the long cubit of 40:5; the district is about 13 by 5 kilometers.
b: The Temple tour counts in a cubit and a handbreadth (40:5; 43:13), usually estimated at about 52 centimeters, or just over 20 inches. By that estimate 25,000 cubits is about 13 kilometers (8 miles), 10,000 is about 5 kilometers (3 miles) and 4,500 about 2.3 kilometers (1.5 miles). These are estimates; the length of the cubit is debated. The numbers are far larger than the Temple area of chapters 40-42, but small beside the land.

a: The sanctuary, the most holy place
p: 'Most holy' of the district, not just of the inner room.
b: The Hebrew is qodesh qodashim, 'holy of holies'. In the Temple it names the inner room (41:4), but here it names the district's holy core. This follows 43:12, which calls the whole area around the top of the mountain most holy. The Plain says 'most holy' for both.

p: The Hebrew is hard; Swete's Greek has cities to live in.
b: The Hebrew has 'twenty rooms' (lishkot), a word used of the Temple's chambers (42:1-14). A Levite district with twenty rooms is odd. Swete's Greek has 'cities to live in', which some commentators take as the sign of a different Hebrew text ('arim lashevet). The Plain follows the Hebrew; see the variant.

t: Land for the leader, and a limit on him
p: Two strips on either side, so that he does not have to take from the tribes.
b: The leader's land is two strips, one on each side of the holy district and the city, running to the east and west borders (48:21-22). With the district and the city between them, the two strips fill the width from the western border to the eastern border, the same length as one tribal portion; neither strip alone runs the whole way. Its purpose is stated in 45:8: so that the leaders no longer oppress the people. Compare Samuel's warning about what a king would take from the people's fields (1 Samuel 8:14) and Ahab's seizure of Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21). Ezekiel's rule that a leader may give away only his own land (46:18) is the legal side of the same idea.

p: The leaders are warned in the words of the earlier prophets against royal injustice.
b: The call to 'do justice and righteousness' and stop evictions echoes the charges against Judah's kings in Jeremiah 22:13-17 and against the shepherds in Ezekiel 34:1-10. The Hebrew pair chamas vashod is 'violence and plunder' (Jeremiah 6:7 and Amos 3:10 pair the same two words). The plural 'leaders' shows that Ezekiel speaks to the whole line of rulers, past and future, not to one person. Isaiah 5:8 and Micah 2:2 attack the same land-grabbing.

p: Leviticus 19:35-36 gives the same demand, and so do Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Amos and Micah.
b: The demand for right scales, a right ephah and a right bath matches the law (Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-15) and the prophets who attacked cheating with small ephahs and heavy shekels (Amos 8:5; Micah 6:10-11). The same word tsedeq, 'right', is used as in Leviticus 19:36.

p: The ephah (dry) and the bath (liquid) are the same size, a tenth of a homer.
b: The ephah measured grain and the bath liquids, and Ezekiel says they hold the same, one tenth of a homer. A homer is then ten ephahs. The usual estimate for the ephah is about 22 liters (around 6 gallons), though scholars differ and no ancient jar settles it. The hin used for oil is a sixth of a bath.

p: The list of weights adds to sixty; Swete's Greek's numbers differ.
b: The Hebrew gives twenty, twenty-five and fifteen shekels for a mina, which adds up to sixty. Sixty fits the Babylonian system, where the mina was sixty shekels. In some other places a mina was fifty shekels. The numbers in Swete's Greek are different and its middle phrase is incomplete, so they do not give the same sum (see the variant). Since the verse starts by stating that a shekel is twenty gerahs (Exodus 30:13), the numbers may reflect a damaged text. Readers disagree whether to correct it.

a: Here is the gift you must set aside
p: Small rates: one-sixtieth of grain, one-hundredth of oil, one in 200 sheep.
b: The rates are low: a sixth of an ephah from each homer of grain is one-sixtieth, a tenth of a bath from each cor of oil is one-hundredth, and one sheep in 200 is half of one percent. These are not tithes (which are a tenth, Numbers 18:21-24). They are the people's gifts to the leader, so that he can meet the cost of the offerings (45:17). Compare the heavy royal takings of 1 Samuel 8:15-17.

p: The offerings cover the people's sins and do not require them to come each time.
b: 'Make atonement' is kipper, the verb of the priests' sacrifices (Leviticus 4:20). Here the offerings that atone are paid for by the people's contribution and handed to the priests by the leader. Swete's Greek has the people's contributions called 'from all the families of Israel'; see the variant.

a: burnt offerings, the grain offerings and the drink offerings
t: The king's old duty, now the leader's
p: Kings once supplied the festival offerings; Ezekiel gives the task to the leader.
b: Solomon offered thousands of sacrifices at the Temple's dedication (1 Kings 8:62-64), and Hezekiah gave from his own flocks for the daily and festival offerings (2 Chronicles 31:3). Ezekiel does not take that away from the ruler, but he limits him: the leader pays for the offerings and does not offer them himself, and the priests do the offering (46:2).

t: Purifying the sanctuary: where is the Day of Atonement?
p: Ezekiel has a New Year and a seventh-day cleansing but no Day of Atonement.
b: In the Torah the sanctuary is cleansed once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Ezekiel has a cleansing on the first day of the first month and another (in the Hebrew, on the seventh day) of the same month, and none in the seventh month. The Talmud asks about it. Menachot 45a asks why 45:18 says 'purify' for a bull that the new-moon rules treat as a burnt offering; Rabbi Yochanan calls the passage difficult and says Elijah will explain it, and Rav Ashi ties it to the offerings at the rededication in Ezra's day. Some critical scholars think the Day of Atonement did not yet exist in this form when Ezekiel wrote; others see his rite as a different ritual for the same purpose.

a: on the seventh day of the month
p: Hebrew says 'the seventh'; Swete's Greek says the first day of the seventh month.
b: The Hebrew has 'on the seventh' (of the month), with no month named. Swete's Greek has 'in the seventh month, on the first of the month'. Menachot 45a asks what the seventh day of the month is for, since no offering is fixed for the seventh day of any month. Rabbi Yochanan reads the verse as the bull for an error of the whole community (Leviticus 4:13-21). The Greek reading would place a second cleansing at the start of the autumn month, where Leviticus 23:24 puts the day of blowing. See the variant.

p: The Hebrew says 'weeks of days'; Swete's Greek has no 'weeks', and the festival is Unleavened Bread.
b: The Hebrew is chag shevu'ot yamim, 'a festival, weeks of days'. Weeks (Shavuot) is a separate festival fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15-21), and Ezekiel does not list it. The word here seems to mean 'a seven (of days)', as in Daniel 10:2-3, where 'weeks of days' means three full weeks. Swete's Greek omits the word 'weeks'. Notice also that Ezekiel's Passover has no lamb and no family meal; it has a bull for the leader and the people (45:22), unlike Exodus 12 and Numbers 28:16-25. A common proposal is to read shiv'at, 'seven of', for shevu'ot, which gives 'a festival of seven days'.

a: seven flawless bulls and seven flawless rams
p: Ezekiel's festival offerings differ from Numbers 28-29.
b: For each day of Unleavened Bread Numbers 28:19-22 asks for two bulls, one ram, seven lambs and a goat. Ezekiel asks for seven bulls, seven rams and a goat, with no lambs. The grain offerings also differ: an ephah per bull or ram here, against three or two tenths of an ephah in Numbers 28. These differences are the heart of the old problem of how to harmonize Ezekiel with the Torah. The Talmud tells how Hananiah ben Hezekiah worked on this in an upper room (Shabbat 13b; Menachot 45a).

a: At the festival in the seventh month
t: The autumn festival and what is missing
p: The festival is Booths, but it is not named; Ezekiel has no Weeks and no Day of Atonement.
b: The fifteenth day of the seventh month is the first day of the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:34), though Ezekiel does not give its name or its booths. The Day of Atonement (tenth day, Leviticus 16; 23:27) and the Feast of Weeks (Leviticus 23:15-21) do not appear in Ezekiel's calendar at all. Ezekiel gives Booths the same offerings as Passover week. Dispensationalist readers who expect these rites in a future Temple, and critical scholars who see an earlier or later stage of the calendar, treat the gaps differently.

a: on the day of the new moon
p: The new moon was a monthly holy day, kept alongside the Sabbath in the prophets.
b: The new moon (the first day of each month) was a day of rest and sacrifice (Numbers 28:11-15; 2 Kings 4:23; Amos 8:5; Isaiah 1:13). Ezekiel pairs it with the Sabbath throughout. His Sabbath offering is six lambs and a ram (46:4), against two lambs in Numbers 28:9-10. His new moon offering is one bull, six lambs and a ram (46:6), against two bulls, a ram and seven lambs in Numbers 28:11. The Talmud counts these among the differences that nearly led the sages to withdraw the book (Shabbat 13b).

a: he will bow down at the gate's threshold
p: The leader worships at the threshold; he does not go farther in.
b: The east gate of the inner court is opened for the leader to stand at the gatepost while the priests offer. He bows low at the threshold and goes out again; the people bow at the doorway. He may not go in to the altar, unlike a priest. The Hebrew verb, hishtachavah, means to bow low to the ground. Uzziah, a king who tried to offer incense, was struck with skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16-21), and the leader is kept from doing this.

a: whatever he is able to give
t: A gift as far as the hand reaches
p: Hebrew: 'the gift of his hand', as much as he can afford.
b: With the ram the grain is fixed (an ephah), but with the lambs the leader gives 'the gift of his hand', as much as he can. The phrase recalls Deuteronomy 16:17, 'each with the gift of his hand'. It fits Ezekiel's rule that the leader provides for the offerings, but it leaves the amount to him.

t: A one-way route through the court
p: A traffic rule that keeps worshipers moving around the court and away from the holy side.
b: On the great festivals people enter by the north gate and leave by the south, or the reverse. The rule keeps a crowd moving in one direction and keeps anyone from turning back toward the entrance. Mishnah Middot 2:2 describes a custom of circling the Temple Mount in one direction. The text does not give its reason; avoiding crowding, and not turning back toward the sanctuary, are the reasons usually proposed.

p: The gate is opened for a freewill offering, just as on the Sabbath.
b: A freewill offering (nedavah) is a gift that nobody requires (Leviticus 22:18-23; Numbers 15:3). When the leader gives one, the east gate is opened for him as on a Sabbath. The Hebrew says 'someone will open', unnamed, so the gate stays under the priests' control. The gate is shut again behind him, as in 44:2 it is shut for good.

t: The daily offering, once a day
p: Ezekiel has one lamb each morning; Exodus and Numbers have two, morning and evening.
b: Exodus 29:38-42 and Numbers 28:3-8 call for two lambs each day, one in the morning and one at twilight, with a tenth of an ephah of flour and a quarter hin of oil. Ezekiel asks for one lamb, every morning only, with a sixth of an ephah of flour and a third of a hin of oil. Swete's Greek has the same. The 'continual' (tamid) offering was the daily rite of the Second Temple, and here it is part of the new order too.

p: Probably the Jubilee, when land went back to its family (Leviticus 25:10).
b: Deror, 'release', is the word for the Jubilee's freedom (Leviticus 25:10), and Isaiah 61:1 and Jeremiah 34:8 use it for the freeing of slaves. The leader's servant may keep a gift of land only until then. It shows that Ezekiel assumes the Jubilee law, or at least the principle that land stays with the family that holds it by inheritance.

a: boil the guilt offering and the sin offering
t: Cooking holy food in the right place
p: The priests' share of the offerings is cooked in a place where no one else can be touched by it.
b: The priests eat the sin offering and the guilt offering (44:29; Leviticus 6:26; 7:6), and the grain offering is baked. Boiling is in the law for the sin offering's meat (Leviticus 6:28). Cooking it in the priests' own rooms means no holy food is carried out to the people, who could be harmed by holiness they are not prepared for (44:19). The people's sacrifices are cooked in separate kitchens (46:24).

p: The word for these courtyards occurs only here; 'closed in' is the usual guess.
b: The Hebrew qeturot is found only here. 'Closed in' is a guess from its root, which usually means 'make smoke' or 'burn incense'; a link with kitchens is only a guess. Swete's Greek has 'small'. The courtyards are corner kitchens, 40 by 30 cubits, with hearths set under rows of stone.

a: Water was flowing out from beneath the threshold
p: A river of life from God's house runs through the Bible, from Eden to the New Jerusalem.
b: A river flows out of Eden and divides into four (Genesis 2:10-14). Psalm 46:4 has a river whose streams make glad the city of God, and Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8 have waters flowing from the LORD's house or from Jerusalem in the last days. Ezekiel's river rises under the Temple's east threshold, south of the altar, and flows toward the sea. In the New Testament John 7:37-39 uses the image for the Spirit, and Revelation 22:1-2 has the river flow from the throne of God and the Lamb. Jerusalem had no river; its water was the Gihon spring in the Kidron Valley.
r: Genesis 2:10-14; Psalm 46:4; Isaiah 33:21; Joel 3:18; Zechariah 14:8; John 7:37-39; Revelation 22:1-2

t: A river that grows without tributaries
p: Each thousand cubits the water rises: ankles, knees, hips, deep enough to swim.
b: The guide measures the river four times, 1,000 cubits each, and each time the water is deeper, although no stream joins it. The growth is a sign that the water carries something from the sanctuary, not from the land. Commentators read the steps as the growth of the LORD's presence or blessing going out from the Temple; the text only says that it rises.

p: The Hebrew names the eastern 'district'; Swete's Greek says Galilee.
b: Gelilah means a 'circuit' or district (Joshua 13:2; 22:10-11). The 'eastern district' is probably the land between Jerusalem and the Jordan valley, the Judean wilderness. Swete's Greek translates it as 'Galilee toward the east', which is a different region altogether in the north. The water is going down toward the rift valley, the Arabah, which runs from the Sea of Galilee through the Jordan and the Salt Sea and on to the Gulf of Aqaba.

a: when it is poured out into the sea
p: The Hebrew of this clause is hard; the Plain gives the sense.
b: The Hebrew says, word for word, 'toward the sea, to the sea, the ones brought out'. It is not clear who 'the ones brought out' are, and the repeated 'to the sea' may be a copyist's repetition. Swete's Greek reads 'to the sea, to the water of the outlet'. The Plain takes the clause to mean the river's water being poured out into the Dead Sea.

p: The same verb Elisha used when he healed the spring at Jericho.
b: 'Healed' is rapha'. Elisha used it of the spring at Jericho, whose bad water he made good with salt (2 Kings 2:19-22). Here the 'sea' is the Salt Sea, the Dead Sea, more than 400 meters below sea level and so salty that fish cannot live in it. Ezekiel's picture is a reversal of the one place in Israel that stands for death. In the Hebrew, the word 'healed' comes back for the water (47:8, 9), and the marshes that are not healed (47:11).

p: A dual form in Hebrew; Swete's Greek has 'the river'.
b: The Hebrew has nachalayim, a dual form, 'two torrents'. The Plain's sentence, 'wherever the two rivers reach', means everywhere the water goes. The dual might mean the two arms of the river, or the river with its branches, or it might be a mistaken doubling of the word. Swete's Greek has 'the river', which is also what the end of the verse says. The Plain keeps the dual, with a variant.

t: Places on the Dead Sea shore
p: En-gedi is on the west shore; En-eglaim is not certainly identified.
b: En-gedi is an oasis on the western shore of the Salt Sea (Joshua 15:62; 1 Samuel 24:1). En-eglaim is named only here and is not certainly known; suggestions include Ein Feshkha on the north-west shore and Ein Hajlah near the mouth of the Jordan, and none is certain. The two names mark a long stretch of shore. Swete's Greek spells them Engaddein and Enagaleim. The Hebrew says only that the fishermen stand 'by it', and the nearest noun is the sea, so the Plain says so.

p: A small part of the shore is not healed: it stays as salt flats.
b: The marshes are left unhealed and 'given to salt', as salt pans. Salt was valuable: it was gathered here in antiquity (Zephaniah 2:9 calls Moab and Ammon 'salt pits'). Readers have taken the detail as a sign that the healing keeps the shore useful, or as a warning that the blessing does not reach every place.

a: every kind of tree that gives food
p: Fruit every month and healing leaves: the Garden and Revelation 22.
b: The trees bear fresh fruit 'for its months', a new crop every month, because the water comes from the sanctuary. Psalm 1:3 and Jeremiah 17:8 picture the righteous as trees by water. Revelation 22:2 has the tree of life on both sides of the river, bearing twelve crops, a fruit each month, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Genesis 2:9 had the tree of life in the garden. The word for 'healing' is terufah, which can also mean medicine.

a: People will eat the fruit, and the leaves will bring healing
t: Reading the river: a future event, or a picture?
p: Literal, spiritual and critical readings of the river.
b: Some Jewish readers who expect a rebuilt Temple, and many Christian Dispensationalists, read the river as a real river in a future age (Zechariah 14:4 says the Mount of Olives will split, and Zechariah 14:8 has living waters flowing from Jerusalem). Many Christians have read it spiritually: as the grace that flows from Christ and the church, as John 7:38 reads the image, and in baptism; the Catholic Easter season sings the antiphon Vidi aquam, 'I saw water flowing from the right side of the temple'. Critical scholars see an ideal picture of Eden restored, set in a landscape Ezekiel's hearers knew.

p: Ezekiel's borders follow Numbers 34 in the north and south but leave out the east bank of the Jordan.
b: Numbers 34:1-15 draws the borders of Canaan; Ezekiel's northern line (Hethlon, Lebo-hamath, Zedad, Hazar-enan) and southern line (Tamar, Meribath-kadesh, the wadi, the Great Sea) are close to it, and the east border is the Jordan, with nothing for the tribes who settled across it in Numbers 32. Several places, such as Hethlon and Sibraim, cannot now be located with certainty. Solomon's kingdom is described in a similar way, 'from Lebo-hamath to the Wadi of Egypt' (1 Kings 8:65).

a: Joseph will receive two measured portions
p: Ephraim and Manasseh each get a strip, as Jacob adopted them.
b: Jacob made Joseph's two sons his own, with a share each (Genesis 48:5), and so Joseph's tribe counts twice, as Ephraim and Manasseh (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). Levi, who takes no land, is not counted, so the tribes still number twelve. The Hebrew has chavalim, 'cords', the measuring lines used in dividing land, in the plural and with no 'two'; the Plain's 'two measured portions' comes from 48:4-5, where Manasseh and Ephraim, Joseph's sons, have a strip each.

a: within which you will give the land out
t: The land: literal, ideal, or promise?
p: Churches and Jews read Ezekiel's borders in different ways; the text names no modern country.
b: Three readings can be told apart. Dispensationalist and many Christian Zionist writers take the borders as a promise still to be kept for the Jewish people. Reformed amillennial writers, such as Hoekema, read the land as the new creation and point to Romans 4:13, where Abraham inherits 'the world'. Critical scholars read it as an ideal map for the returning exiles that was never drawn on the ground. Ezekiel's borders do not match any modern state's, and it is a choice of interpretation to apply them.

t: Seas, a wadi and a verb
p: The last word of 47:18 is a verb in the Hebrew, 'you will measure'; Swete's Greek has a place name.
b: Hebrew uses 'sea' for the west. The Great Sea is the Mediterranean (Numbers 34:6). The eastern sea is the Salt Sea or Dead Sea. 'The wadi' in 47:19 is the Wadi of Egypt, which Numbers 34:5 and Isaiah 27:12 name. The last word of 47:18 in the Hebrew is tammodu, 'you will measure' (תָּמֹדּוּ), and the Plain translates it so. Swete's Greek has Phoinikonos, 'of the palm grove', which stands for Tamar (tamar means 'date palm'), the place named in 47:19 and 48:28. Reading Tamar here would mean a change of one letter (resh for dalet) and of the ending. The Hebrew as it stands is a rough sentence, and no Hebrew witness read for this part has Tamar. See the variant.

a: the foreigners who live among you
p: Resident foreigners with children get an inheritance, in contrast with 44:9.
b: The Hebrew ger is a resident foreigner, not the ben nekhar of 44:9. Ezekiel allows a ger who has children to be treated like a native-born Israelite and to receive land in the tribe where he lives, which no earlier law says (compare Leviticus 19:33-34 and Numbers 15:15-16, which give equal treatment but no land). Isaiah 56:3-8 welcomes foreigners to the Temple, which Ezekiel 44:9 does not. How these fit together is debated: 44:9 deals with the uncircumcised, 47:22 with foreigners who have become part of the community.

p: Dan at the far north, Gad at the far south; the order is Ezekiel's own.
b: The tribes are laid out in seven strips north of the holy district and five south, each running from the east border to the west. The order is not Joshua's. Three of the four sons of the maidservants (Dan, Asher, Naphtali) are in the north, followed by Joseph's two sons, Reuben and Judah. Judah and Benjamin flank the sanctuary, as Judah and Benjamin held Jerusalem in the older land (Joshua 15:8; 18:16). Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun and Gad lie to the south. Some tribes keep roughly their old region: Asher and Naphtali in the north, Judah and Benjamin around Jerusalem. Others move. Dan, which lay by the coast south-west of Benjamin in Joshua 19:40-48, is placed at the far north (Judges 18 tells of a Danite move north). Reuben and Gad, who settled east of the Jordan (Numbers 32), receive strips west of it. Issachar and Zebulun, northern tribes in Joshua, are placed in the south.

a: the contribution you will set apart
t: The sums for the holy district
p: The totals in 45:1, 48:9 and 48:13 fail in the Hebrew and work only with Swete's Greek's numbers.
b: The district is 25,000 by 25,000 cubits (48:20): 10,000 for the priests (with the sanctuary), 10,000 for the Levites, and 5,000 for the city and its land (48:10, 13, 15). That adds up only if the priests' and Levites' strips are each 10,000 wide, as 45:3, 45:5, 48:10 and 48:13 say in the Hebrew. But the Hebrew totals fail in three places. In 45:1 the whole holy contribution is 25,000 by 10,000, which cannot hold two strips of that size. In 48:13 the two strips together are called 25,000 by 10,000 'in all', though side by side they are 20,000 wide. And 48:9 uses the words of 48:8, 'the contribution that you set apart', for a strip 10,000 wide, where 48:8 and 48:20 use them for the whole square. The Plain follows the Hebrew everywhere; see the notes and variants at 48:9 and 48:13. Verse 8 says the district is as long, east to west, as a tribal portion, while verse 20 calls it a square, so commentators draw the map in different ways.

a: The contribution that you set apart for the LORD
p: 48:8 and 48:9 use the same Hebrew words for different measures.
b: The Hebrew of 48:9, hatterumah asher tarimu laYHWH, is the phrase of 48:8 and 48:20, where it names the whole district. Here the width is 10,000, which fits the priests' strip of 48:10. The Hebrew does not say 'the part of it'; commentators who read it that way are harmonizing 48:9 with 48:10. The Plain translates the Hebrew words as they stand, and the variant gives Swete's Greek, whose 25,000 makes the verse the whole square.
orig: הַתְּרוּמָה אֲשֶׁר תָּרִימוּ לַיהוָה (hatterumah asher tarimu laYHWH)

a: The whole length is 25,000 and the width 10,000.
t: Where the sums work only on the Greek
p: Swete's Greek gives the totals that make the district add up; the Hebrew does not.
b: Swete's Greek (Vaticanus) reads 20,000 at 45:1 and 48:13, which makes those two totals work, and 25,000 at 48:9, which makes that verse the whole square. So the totals work only on the Greek readings. But the same Greek gives each strip as 20,000 at 45:3 and 45:5, which does not fit its own 45:1, and its 48:10 leaves out the east side. No single text is free of trouble. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, which the strips support (10,000 each in 48:10 and 48:13), and shows each difference in a variant.

p: The reasons given in 44:15 are repeated: faithful priests get the best land.
b: The Zadokites are given the part of the district that holds the sanctuary. The reason is the same as in 44:15-16: they stayed faithful 'when the Israelites went astray'. The Levites, who 'went astray', are given the next strip, and they may not sell it (48:14).

t: The city is common, not holy
p: The city is on ground that is not holy, but it is the LORD's city.
b: The Hebrew chol, 'common', names what is not holy: not unclean, only open to ordinary use (44:23). The city and its fields are kept outside the holy contribution. The text keeps the Temple, the priests and the city apart, and the city's workers farm the land for it and come from every tribe (48:19). The name in 48:35 then says the LORD is in it.

p: About 2.3 kilometers on each side, with open land around it.
b: The city is a square 4,500 cubits on each side, with 250 cubits of open land all around (48:17), so its area with the open land is 5,000 by 5,000. That is about 2.3 kilometers (1.5 miles) a side, not large. Revelation 21:16 has a city that is a cube 12,000 stadia on each side (about 2,200 kilometers). Ezekiel's city has no Temple inside; the Temple lies in the holy district to the north (48:10, 21). Revelation's city has no Temple at all (Revelation 21:22).

a: Reuben's gate, Judah's gate and Levi's gate
p: Three gates on each side, as in Revelation 21:12-13.
b: The twelve gates carry the names of the tribes: north, Reuben, Judah and Levi; east, Joseph, Benjamin and Dan; south, Simeon, Issachar and Zebulun; west, Gad, Asher and Naphtali. Levi is here a tribe with a gate, though it has no strip of land, and Joseph stands for Ephraim and Manasseh. The north and south gates are for sons of Leah, the east gates for sons of Rachel (with Dan, born to her maid), and the west gates for the sons of the two maids. Revelation 21:12-13 also has twelve gates with the names of the twelve tribes, three on each side, but does not give them in this order.

p: The new name of the city, and the last words of the book.
b: The Hebrew is YHWH shammah, 'the LORD [is] there'. It is a sentence used as a name, as Isaiah 7:14 ('God with us') and Jeremiah 33:16 do. It answers the book's central loss: the glory left the Temple (10:18-19; 11:22-23) and came back (43:1-5). The Talmud says three are called by God's name: the righteous, the Messiah and Jerusalem, and it quotes this verse for Jerusalem (Bava Batra 75b). Revelation 21:3 says God will live with his people, and 21:22 says he and the Lamb are the Temple.
